items.prompt: In a word-search branch where a cell cannot be reused, when should the current cell be marked visited?

options.text: After bounds and value checks pass, before exploring neighbors.
Before confirming the coordinates are inside the grid.
Only after all neighbor recursion finishes.
Visited state is unnecessary in path search.

feedback.reason: The current cell becomes part of the active path only after it is proven legal.

blocks.text: Validate first, then claim the cell for the path
Bounds must be checked before reading or writing board[r][c]. Then the cell's target value and current-path availability establish that it is a legal next step.
Only after those checks pass does the call mark the cell. The mark remains visible throughout neighbor recursion so no descendant can reuse it, and it is removed when this call unwinds.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: Out-of-bounds memory cannot be marked safely. Descendants could reuse the current cell. Cycles and cell reuse can violate the path contract.

blocks.title: State transition
blocks.text: Bounds/value/visited checks establish legality; marking then makes the legal cell part of the active route.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.before_bounds: An out-of-bounds coordinate does not identify a valid matrix entry, so reading or marking it is unsafe.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.after_all_neighbors: Without the mark during recursion, a descendant can step back onto the current cell and violate the no-reuse contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.never: Cycles and cell reuse can violate the path contract.

items.prompt: Why is one global visited set usually incorrect when every starting cell should be allowed to begin an independent path search?

options.text: A cell used by one failed path may still be required by another path or starting position.
Global visited works only on large grids.
A set cannot store coordinates.
Recursive search always requires global visited state.

feedback.reason: Visited state belongs to the current path when cells may be reused across different candidate paths.

blocks.text: Visited ownership lasts only for one active route
A path-local visited set represents exactly the cells on the current root-to-node route. When recursion returns, its cell is removed so a sibling route sees the same availability its parent saw.

A global never-clear set instead remembers cells used by completed or failed routes. It can reject a cell needed by a later sibling or independent starting position even though those paths are never active together.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: Grid size is not the issue. A set can store coordinates; the scope is wrong. Path-local state is common.

blocks.title: Scope rule
blocks.text: Match visited-state lifetime to the contract: route-local no-reuse requires restoration between routes.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.grid_too_small: The defect depends on sharing state across independent paths, not on the number of rows or columns.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.visited_cannot_store_cells: A set can store coordinates; the scope is wrong.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.recursion_requires_global: Recursion can pass, mutate-and-restore, or persist branch-local state; it does not require global visitation.

items.prompt: A grid word-search call has already matched every target character. What should happen before attempting another cell access?

options.text: Return success immediately.
Read another cell to confirm the path.
Erase the entire board.
Restart the outer search loop.

feedback.reason: The completion contract is based on target progress, not on making an extra move.

blocks.text: Completion precedes any next-coordinate validation
In the stated call contract, target progress already equals the target length. The current path therefore satisfies the result condition without selecting another cell.

Returning success before bounds or board access is important because the coordinate passed after the final match may be irrelevant or even outside the grid. Cleanup owned by earlier frames still occurs while success unwinds if the public contract requires restoration.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: The target contract is already complete. Completion does not require destructive cleanup. Success may be propagated under a find-one contract.

blocks.title: Base-case order
blocks.text: If all target positions are matched, return success before inspecting a nonexistent next step.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.read_next_cell: The target is already complete, so another access adds no evidence and may use an invalid next coordinate.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.clear_board: Success may require unwinding temporary marks, but erasing the entire immutable input is unrelated destructive mutation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.restart_start_cells: Success may be propagated under a find-one contract.

items.prompt: A cell is marked visited, all neighbor branches fail, and the function returns without unmarking it. What defect results?

options.text: Sibling paths can be incorrectly blocked from using that cell.
Only the order of duplicate outputs changes.
The board becomes sorted.
The target string becomes shorter.

feedback.reason: A failed branch must restore every path-local mark.

blocks.text: A failed route must release its cell
The mark was introduced only to prevent descendants of this branch from reusing the cell. After every neighbor fails, the branch is finished and no longer owns that temporary exclusion.
Returning without unmarking leaks the exclusion into the parent. A later sibling then sees the cell as unavailable and may lose a valid route that uses it from a different prefix.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: The branch may lose valid paths entirely. No sorting occurs. The defect is visited-state leakage.

blocks.title: Leak symptom
blocks.text: If one failed route changes which cells a sibling may use, branch-local state was not fully restored.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.duplicate_output_only: The leaked mark can suppress the only valid sibling path, changing existence and completeness rather than merely output order.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.board_sorted: A boolean mark or sentinel does not compare or reorder row values, so no sorting occurs.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_shortened: The target is unchanged; the defect is that visited-state from a failed route remains visible.

items.prompt: A problem permits four-directional movement only. Which neighbor set is legal from (r, c)?

options.text: (r - 1, c), (r + 1, c), (r, c - 1), and (r, c + 1), subject to bounds.
Only the four diagonal cells.
Every unvisited cell in the grid.
Only (r, c) again.

feedback.reason: Candidate generation begins with the exact movement relation.

blocks.text: Four directions mean one coordinate changes by one
Orthogonal adjacency changes exactly one coordinate by ±1: up (r - 1, c), down (r + 1, c), left (r, c - 1), and right (r, c + 1).

These are candidate coordinates, not automatically legal cells. Bounds, target progress, and current-path visited state filter them before recursion. Diagonal, arbitrary-grid, and same-cell moves violate the stated movement relation.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: The movement contract excludes diagonals. A path step must satisfy adjacency. The current cell cannot be reused as the next step.

blocks.title: Movement rule
blocks.text: Generate from the declared geometry first, then apply state and target filters.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.diagonal_four: A diagonal changes both row and column, while the four-directional contract permits only orthogonal moves.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.all_grid_cells: Being unvisited is insufficient; a next step must also be orthogonally adjacent to the current coordinate.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_cell: The current cell cannot be reused as the next step.

items.prompt: A collect-all contract forbids cell reuse within each path but does not consume cells globally. Why may the same board cell appear in two different successful paths?

options.text: Visited restrictions apply within one path, not necessarily across independent result paths.
Visited state is ignored after the first solution.
Every cell has an implicit duplicate copy.
All result paths are one shared mutable path.

feedback.reason: Path-local visited state prevents cycles and reuse inside a branch while allowing independent branches to use the same resources.

blocks.text: Separate paths may reuse a shared board resource

The prompt defines no-reuse within each path and explicitly says cells are not consumed globally. A visited mark therefore records membership in one active path, not permanent ownership by the first result.
When a successful path is saved as an independent snapshot, recursion restores its marks. A later branch can then use the same physical cell while still obeying its own internal no-reuse rule.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: Each path must still obey no-reuse internally. The same physical cell is reused across separate branches. Results should be independent snapshots.

blocks.title: Resource scope
blocks.text: No-reuse within one result does not imply global consumption across independently returned results.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.visited_ignored: Visited checks remain active inside every path; restoration only allows a different branch to begin from clean state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.cell_duplicates: The same physical cell is reused across separate branches.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.paths_share_state: Returned paths should be independent snapshots; sharing one mutable live path would corrupt stored results.

items.prompt: A solver temporarily replaces board[r][c] with a sentinel to mark it visited. What must happen when the branch returns?
constraints: The sentinel cannot equal any legal board value.

options.text: Restore the original cell value.
Leave the sentinel for all future searches.
Sort the row containing the cell.
Remove the cell from the grid.

feedback.reason: In-place marking is a reversible state representation.

blocks.text: Sentinel marking borrows the board cell temporarily

The frame first saves the original value, then writes a sentinel outside the legal board alphabet. Descendants treat that sentinel as unavailable, implementing current-path visitation without a separate matrix.

Before the frame returns—on failure and on any success path whose public contract preserves the board—it writes the saved value back. Otherwise later branches observe corrupted input and treat the cell as globally blocked.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: That converts path-local visited state into a global block. Sorting is unrelated and changes the board. The grid shape must remain unchanged.

blocks.title: Ownership rule
blocks.text: The frame that overwrites a cell must retain and restore its exact original value.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.leave_sentinel: That converts path-local visited state into a global block.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_row: Sorting changes unrelated positions and destroys the board's spatial meaning rather than reversing the one-cell mutation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.delete_cell: Removing a cell changes grid dimensions and adjacency; restoration requires the original value at the original coordinate.

items.prompt: Why should the outer driver try every grid cell as a potential starting position when no start is specified?

options.text: A valid path may begin at any cell matching the first target condition.
Every recursive function must be called once per cell.
Global visited state requires visiting every cell first.
Trying every cell sorts the grid.

feedback.reason: The first choice is the starting cell.

blocks.text: The unspecified start is the root choice
When no origin is fixed, the result contract permits a valid path to begin at any coordinate satisfying the first target condition. Omitting a coordinate can therefore omit the only valid root.

The outer driver iterates every cell, cheaply skips first-condition mismatches, and launches a fresh path-local search from each remaining candidate. This is a problem-specific completeness requirement, not a universal property of recursion.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: This is problem-specific, not a recursion rule. The outer loop should not globally mark cells. No reordering occurs.

blocks.title: Root coverage
blocks.text: If the start is unspecified, candidate enumeration includes every coordinate that can satisfy the first step.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.recursion_requires_all: Only this problem's unspecified-origin contract requires all candidate starts; recursion itself imposes no once-per-cell rule.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.visited_global: The outer loop should not globally mark cells.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.grid_sorted: Iteration observes coordinates in some order but does not compare or rearrange grid values.

items.prompt: Which checks can reject a grid-search call before marking the current cell? Select all that apply.

options.text: The coordinates are outside the grid.
The cell does not match the required target symbol or predicate.
The cell is already visited by the current path when reuse is forbidden.
A different neighbor failed in an earlier sibling branch.

feedback.reason: Immediate legality checks occur before mutating visited state.

blocks.text: Reject an illegal call before any visited mutation

items: Check bounds before reading board[r][c], because an out-of-range coordinate names no cell.
Check the required symbol or predicate, because a mismatch cannot extend the target prefix.
Check current-path visitation, because reusing the cell violates the no-reuse contract.

blocks.text: Only a call that passes all three checks may mark the cell and explore descendants. A failed earlier sibling is evidence about that sibling's subtree, not about the legality of the same coordinate under a different path prefix.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: One sibling's failure does not invalidate this cell.

blocks.title: Guard order
blocks.text: Completion first when applicable, then bounds, value, and visited checks; mutate only after legality is established.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.neighbor_failed: One sibling's failure does not invalidate this cell.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.out_of_bounds: There is no legal cell to use.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.target_mismatch: The branch cannot represent the target prefix.

items.prompt: Which state must be restored between sibling grid branches when the corresponding mutable representation is used? Select all that apply.

options.text: The current cell's visited mark.
Any temporary sentinel written into the board.
Any coordinate or character appended to the current path.
The immutable target string itself.

feedback.reason: Every mutable branch-local representation must return to the parent state.

blocks.text: Restore every mutable representation actually used

items: Clear a separate visited mark so the sibling receives the parent's visited set.
Replace an in-board sentinel with the exact original cell value.
Remove a coordinate or character appended to the shared live path.

blocks.text: A solver may use a visited matrix or a sentinel rather than both, which is why the prompt conditions each restoration on the representation being present. The immutable target is only read; sharing it creates no mutation to reverse.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: Reading shared immutable input requires no restoration.

blocks.title: Restoration checklist
blocks.text: List the structures changed by this branch and reverse each change before the next sibling.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.immutable_target: The target is immutable configuration shared by all branches; reading it does not alter parent state and requires no restoration.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.visited_mark: Sibling paths need the parent visited set.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.board_sentinel: The original cell value must be restored.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.path_entry: The sibling should inherit only the parent path.

items.prompt: Which tests are important for grid-search visited-state correctness? Select all that apply.

options.text: A one-cell grid with matching and non-matching targets.
A valid path that changes direction.
A target that can match only if a cell is illegally reused.
Only one large random board.

feedback.reason: Minimal, directional, and illegal-reuse cases expose distinct state errors.

blocks.text: A small test matrix isolates distinct failure modes

items: One-cell match and mismatch test completion ordering, minimal bounds, and the first target comparison.
A path that turns verifies enumeration of all four orthogonal directions rather than one straight orientation.
A target achievable only by revisiting a cell must fail, directly testing current-path no-reuse.

blocks.text: Add a case where one route fails before a sibling succeeds to test restoration. A single large random board may exercise many states but gives weak evidence about which boundary or state transition caused a wrong result.

blocks.title: Why the other answers fail
blocks.text: It may not isolate boundary and restoration defects.

blocks.title: Test design rule
blocks.text: Choose inputs whose expected outcome changes when exactly one visited-state invariant is broken.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.only_large_random: It may not isolate boundary and restoration defects.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.single_cell: It tests completion and minimal bounds.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.requires_turn: It verifies neighbor enumeration beyond a straight line.

items.prompt: Arrange the control flow for one grid-search call.

elements.text: Return success if the target is already fully matched.
Reject bounds, mismatch, or path reuse.
Mark the current cell as used by the path.
Search neighbors, then restore the cell before returning.

feedback.reason: Completion, immediate failure, mutation, and recursive expansion have distinct ordering.

blocks.text: One call: complete, validate, own, explore and restore

items: If target progress already equals target length, return success before another coordinate access.
Otherwise reject out-of-bounds coordinates, target mismatch, or reuse by the current path.
Mark the legal cell so every descendant sees it as owned by this route.
Explore neighbors, then restore the cell before either success or failure leaves the frame when the input must remain unchanged.

blocks.text: Each dependency protects a different boundary: completion prevents an unnecessary next access, validation prevents illegal mutation, marking prevents cycles, and restoration isolates siblings.

blocks.title: Why this order matters
blocks.text: The order follows causal dependencies: Return success if the target is already fully matched. Then Reject bounds, mismatch, or path reuse. Then Mark the current cell as used by the path. Then Search neighbors, then restore the cell before returning. Reversing a dependency either evaluates an unprepared state or leaves branch state unrecovered.

blocks.title: Call invariant
blocks.text: Access only an unfinished legal state; recurse only from a marked legal cell; return with owned mutations restored.

items.prompt: Arrange the operations for exploring one legal neighbor.

elements.text: Compute the neighbor coordinates.
Check bounds, target progress, and visited state.
Recurse into the legal neighbor.
Process the result according to find-one or collect-all semantics.

feedback.reason: A neighbor becomes a child branch only after its coordinates and state are legal.

blocks.text: Turn a movement offset into a legal child

items: Apply one allowed movement offset to compute the neighbor coordinates.
Validate bounds, the next target condition, and absence from the current path.
Recurse only if the neighbor is legal.
For find-one, propagate success after required cleanup; for collect-all, save results and continue other legal neighbors.

blocks.text: Coordinates must exist before validation, and validation must precede recursion. The final response is not fixed by recursion itself; it follows the declared result semantics.

blocks.title: Why this order matters
blocks.text: The order follows causal dependencies: Compute the neighbor coordinates. Then Check bounds, target progress, and visited state. Then Recurse into the legal neighbor. Then Process the result according to find-one or collect-all semantics. Reversing a dependency either evaluates an unprepared state or leaves branch state unrecovered.

blocks.title: Child boundary
blocks.text: Movement proposes coordinates; legality checks decide whether they become a recursive branch.

items.prompt: Arrange the reversible in-place marking sequence for a cell.

elements.text: Save the original cell value.
Replace it with a visited sentinel.
Explore all legal descendants of the current path.
Write the original value back before returning.

feedback.reason: In-place marking must preserve enough information to reverse the mutation.

blocks.text: Save before overwrite, restore after descendants

items: Read and save the original legal cell value.
Write the noncolliding sentinel to mark the cell as owned by this path.
Explore descendants while the sentinel remains visible.
Write the saved value back before the frame returns.

blocks.text: Overwriting before saving destroys the only restoration value. Restoring before recursion permits illegal reuse; omitting restoration leaks the branch marker into siblings and the caller.

blocks.title: Why this order matters
blocks.text: The order follows causal dependencies: Save the original cell value. Then Replace it with a visited sentinel. Then Explore all legal descendants of the current path. Then Write the original value back before returning. Reversing a dependency either evaluates an unprepared state or leaves branch state unrecovered.

blocks.title: Reversibility rule
blocks.text: An in-place marker is safe only when the exact old value is retained and restored on every required return path.

items.prompt: Arrange the outer search over unspecified starting cells.

elements.text: Iterate every grid coordinate.
Skip starts that cannot match the first target condition.
Run a fresh path-local backtracking search from the candidate start.
Return early for find-one or accumulate results for collect-all.

feedback.reason: The start position is the root choice of each independent path search.

blocks.text: Enumerate every legal root, with fresh route state

items: Iterate every coordinate because the start is unspecified.
Skip cells that cannot satisfy the first target condition.
Launch path-local backtracking from each remaining root with no marks leaked from prior starts.
Return after first success for find-one, or accumulate independent results and continue for collect-all.

blocks.text: First-condition filtering is safe because a mismatching cell cannot be a valid root. Fresh route state is essential because a cell used below one root may be required below another.

blocks.title: Why this order matters
blocks.text: The order follows causal dependencies: Iterate every grid coordinate. Then Skip starts that cannot match the first target condition. Then Run a fresh path-local backtracking search from the candidate start. Then Return early for find-one or accumulate results for collect-all. Reversing a dependency either evaluates an unprepared state or leaves branch state unrecovered.

blocks.title: Driver invariant
blocks.text: Every eligible coordinate becomes a root exactly as required by the result contract, and no root inherits another's path state.

items.prompt: Arrange failure unwinding after all neighbors of a marked cell fail.

elements.text: Determine that no neighbor completed the target.
Restore the current cell's visited state and remove any path entry.
Confirm the mutable state again matches the parent branch.
Report failure to the parent branch.

feedback.reason: The parent must receive failure together with its original branch state.

blocks.text: Failure propagates only after state is repaired

items: Conclude that every legal neighbor of the current marked cell failed.
Restore all state owned by this frame: the cell mark or sentinel and any live path entry.
Verify that the mutable visited and path representations again equal the parent state.
Return failure so the parent may safely try another sibling.

blocks.text: Unmarking and popping need not have an arbitrary order when they are independent; they form one restoration obligation. What is causally required is that both finish before failure is observable to the parent.

blocks.title: Why this order matters
blocks.text: Returning immediately after neighbor exhaustion leaks state. Treating unmark and pop as globally ordered also teaches a false dependency; the actual invariant is complete restoration before return.

blocks.title: Failure contract
blocks.text: The parent receives both the failure result and its exact original mutable state.

items.prompt: A grid has R·C possible starting cells, the target length is L, and each step considers at most four neighbors. Select a standard loose worst-case time bound and recursion depth.
constraints: A cell cannot be reused within one path.
The bound may ignore the reduced branching after the first step.

feedback.reason: Each starting cell can launch an exponential path search bounded by target length.

blocks.text: Multiply possible roots by a loose path tree
There are R·C candidate starting cells. From each start, the deliberately loose model permits at most four choices for each of at most L target positions, giving no more than 4^L path sequences.

Multiplying roots by per-root exploration yields O(RC·4^L). No-reuse makes immediate reversal and exhausted cells unavailable, so tighter analyses often use a smaller effective factor, but the prompt explicitly asks for the standard safe loose bound.

One active recursive route matches at most one character per level and stops after L positions, so recursion depth is O(L). The exponential number of alternative routes is not simultaneously present on the call stack.

blocks.title: Check each dimension independently
blocks.text: O(RC·L) assumes only one continuation per level. O((RC)^L) incorrectly allows a jump to any grid cell at each step rather than one of four neighbors.

blocks.title: Complexity rule
blocks.text: Count roots, multiply by the branch tree per root, and count only one route for recursion depth.

items.prompt: A grid search uses an explicit R by C visited matrix and recursion depth at most L, excluding the immutable board and returned results. Select the auxiliary-space bound.
constraints: The visited matrix remains allocated for the search.
Only one depth-first path is active at a time.

feedback.reason: The explicit visited representation and recursion stack both contribute.

blocks.text: Add persistent visited storage and the live call stack
The explicit visited matrix has one entry per cell and remains allocated, contributing O(RC) space. Depth-first recursion keeps at most L active frames because one character is matched per level.
The independent contributions add to O(RC + L). Neither O(RC) nor O(L) alone accounts for both declared representations, and the immutable board and returned results are excluded by the prompt.

If the implementation instead uses reversible sentinels in the board, the separate O(RC) matrix can disappear, leaving O(L) stack space under the same exclusions. That is a different representation from the one asked about.

blocks.title: Check each dimension independently
blocks.text: Time spent exploring branches does not allocate one visited matrix per branch; the single matrix is reused and restored. Conversely, one active path does not eliminate the matrix's persistent allocation.

blocks.title: Space rule
blocks.text: Sum simultaneously live representations: O(RC) visited state plus O(L) recursive frames.
